I cut AMD some slack for their continued pricing strategy for the following reason.  

If all things were equal between AMD and Nvidia hardware (performance, price, etc), if given the option, the decades of having a monopoly on GPUs would show through with most consumers likely picking Nvidia hardware.  

AMD runs high risk by making it's margins really thin compared to Nvidia.  If they do this for an entire generation of GPUs, they run the risk of Nvidia responding with affordable/good value hardware.  And because most people I still think would prefer Nvidia it could really cause a tough next generation (whatever follows 9000 series) GPUs for AMD.  I get the strategy of making the money while you can, slowly try build a faithful fan base, a fan base that won't jump back to team green as soon as there is a good value option from them.

comments.text:
@stanley3647  yes and no, memory bandwidth is mainly a bus width. the RTX 3070FE has a 256bit memory bus over 8 chips, the 9060XT for both 8GB and 16GB models have a 128bit bus spread over 8/16 chips. so of course, the 9060XT is memory starved because of it's bus width. there's plenty of titles that favor it, and plenty of other titles that don't care about bandwidth. keep in mind, memory bandwidth is NOT a function of the PCIe lanes, as you can run a 5090 on 8 PCIe lanes and only loose 1-2% performance.

Why would you want 16GB in a "slower" card? maybe people balance between games and light productivity? some games can use more than 8GB, and when talking about 3D modling and texturing, these can use massive amounts of VRAM as well. also, Virtual Reality, this is more framebuffer and core frequency driven than really any flatscreen title collection ever dreamed to be, and where that 16GB will be king over the 8GB cards.

An excellent unbiased review comparing the 9060xt to the 5060. I like the way you make fair statements and don't take anything personal. You're right and the 9060xt is a better card simply because of its performance vs price in the category it was intended.

A personal perspective I'd like to share is that the saying "frames win games" is the key motivation for these technology companies. They know that people have money to invest in more performance and they do have an obligation to maximize a product lineup. It can be understood that silicon manufacturing has gotten really expensive since the hype of PC gaming has been driven up so it's important for these companies to maximize their yield on the wafer. With that in mind the card manufacturers also have an obligation to maintain production and fulfill their obligations to the component manufacturers. It's a sensitive economy so just remember that when a product doesn't meet a consumers expectation it's likely because they want you to buy something bigger and better. The best way to sell a product sometimes is to give them a product for $350 that they don't want so they buy the $700 product that they've been told they need; that product is Frames Per Second. Features my dear Jay; they are selling features and the peripherals that you need to utilize those features. Unfortunately the tech reviewers have done a great job of motivating the consumers to chase the frames instead of enjoying the playability of the games with whatever hardware that is available.

I think we can mostly infer what that'd be like from past reviews and comparisons of those technologies: In terms of quality, games that support DLSS4 will look slightly better on the GeForce GPU with upscaling, while games that support FSR4 not quite, but will look perfectly viable now even at 1080p, somewhere between DLSS3 and 4 quality. Performance wise the similarly named quality levels are roughly the same perf uplifts between Radeon and Nvidia. Frame gen is quality wise quite comparable between the two. However AMD only does 2x frames, Nvidia gives you 3x in supported games, if even more fake frames are your cup of tea. 

The most significant difference between the two cards compared here will be the memory limit. All these technologies require extra VRAM, so with the 5060 in games that are already on the edge of 8GB usage, you might actually tank frame rates enabling them, while the 9060XT has no issues with that. That of course applies to any comparison between the various 8GB/16GB models from both vendors.

comments.text: This is a biased review, I'm sorry. You're directly comparing a 16gb model to an 8gb model. While the price parody is there, the capabilities just aren't, and in all those tests where you had the 5060 16gb model, you could see it pull ahead every time. The fact that their 8gb model could keep up where it mattered for the targeted area meant that, for very specific use cases revolving around entry level gameplay at 1080 and 1440p, it doesn't matter who you chose. While the 9060 XT and 5060 16gb model will last much longer in terms of when you need to upgrade, the 5060 16gb will last even longer than the 9060 XT due to increased horsepower of the card. HOWEVER, the reality is that if you want a good entry level card, the two main competitors are not who you should be comparing at all, but the B580 is. Their card seems to be the ultimate price to performance at entry level, and should always be on every list going forward regardless of how you feel about intel at all. With the B580 hitting ALL of the price point arguments and not even having an 8GB option, just the one 12GB option because, lets be honest, 12GB is just enough to not need to worry about your entry card being DOA when attempting to use it with the titles that are out now. Is it perfect? No! But is it in the exact price point that every entry level gamer wants it to be at? Yes. It's exemplifying the "good enough" mindset. It's good enough for what it needs to be, and compared to other cards which are aiming for performance perfection, we're all forgetting that entry level gamers don't want perfect. They don't want "the best." They want something good enough to give them a taste, or allow them to continue on casually without needing to worry about an upgrade in the immediate future. Remember Jay, mo competition, mo betta. Even if the competition is behind on most metrics, if they're an option that makes sense for entry level or younger gamers, they're a viable option. Always bring all facets of the competition to the table, though if Valve got into the GPU market on the budget end of things, we might see some really wild competition.

That's the thing. Yes, the 9060 16GB WILL last longer than the 5060 8GB, you won't NEED to buy a new card when the next gen comes out even if you're on the low end of the market so long as it has those 16 gigs, but you also won't NEED a new card if it has 12 gigs for at least a gen or two as well, hence my mention of the B580. Price to performance, blow to blow, the B580 can do everything an entry card needs to do, and a few things it doesn't actually need to, and will remain useable for the next couple of generations. Is the 5060 8GB an absolute sham and a total scam? Yes. Yet, does it do all the things an entry card needs to do by all the metrics we can measure by on its launch? It excels at them, even. Price fixing is an agreement between competitors to artificially prop up prices.

If Toyota announces a higher price for the new, next-gen Corolla, then Honda looks at that and next model year puts out a refreshed Civic and raises the price within a couple hundred bucks of Toyota, they have not engaged in price fixing. Simply seeing what a competitor is doing and following their lead is not illegal. 

If the price of ECUs from a third party supplier to both companies goes up, and both companies decide to pass through the price increase, they have not engaged in price fixing. Having the same cost structure as a competitor and getting hit with the same shocks is not illegal. 

If the CEOs called each other and discussed the plan, that would be price fixing.
